To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the protein-sparing effect of either glucose (4 g/hour) or lipid (20% Intrilipid) infusion in surgical patients was governed by the patient's clinical disease state and not by the specific substrate infused.
the infusion of glucose or lipid is equally effective as a protein-sparing therapy in patients with sepsis and trauma, and with lower gastrointestinal cancer.
the protein-sparing effect of a given amount of substrate infusion is determined by the clinical state of the patient, and is not determined by the specific type of substrate infused.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the infusion of glucose and lipid calories on the metabolic response to surgery.
the metabolic response to trauma and/or sepsis.
the metabolic response to injury, and the effect of various therapeutic interventions on the response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in surgical patients with either upper or lower gastrointestinal cancer, the infusion of either lipid or glucose is equally effective as a protein-sparing therapy.

the infusion of either fat or glucose in the amounts used in the study is effective in suppressing the ongoing rate of protein catabolisms in the three patient groups, but the magnitude of the effect is governed by the disease state.
the protein-sparing effect of either glucose, or fat, or both is governed by the severity of the catabolic response, which in turn is governed by the underlying disease state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of either lipid or glucose infusion on rates of net protein catabism is not determined by the individual substrate but rather by the disease state.
the protein-sparing effect of either glucose of lipid is dependent upon the clinical disease state, and not upon the individual substrate infused.

the protein-sparing effect of glucose or fat infusion is governed by the severity of the underlying disease state, and that the degree of protein catabolisis that occurs despite substrate infusion is directly related to the severity of the clinical state of the patient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the protein-sparing effect of either glucose, or fat is governed by the disease state of the individual patient, and not by a specific substrate.
the protein-sparing effect of a substrate infusion is determined by the clinical condition of the patient and not by the nature of the substrate infused.
the infusion of calories as glucose or fat can be equally effective as a protein-sparing intervention in the surgical patient.
